items.title: A nil error that is not nil
items.question: func find() error { var e *MyErr = nil; return e }. The caller checks err != nil and it is true. Why?
items.answer: An interface value is a (dynamic type, value) pair. Returning a typed nil pointer produces an interface whose type is *MyErr and whose value is nil, which does not equal the nil interface. Return a literal nil on the success path.

source.name: Go FAQ - Why is my nil error value not equal to nil?

items.title: Goroutine scheduling
items.body: The Go runtime multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads; GOMAXPROCS sets how many threads execute Go code simultaneously. Goroutines start with small, growable stacks and the scheduler can preempt long-running ones, so huge numbers of goroutines are cheap.
items.question: What happens to other goroutines when one makes a blocking system call?
items.answer: The runtime detaches the blocked thread and lets another thread run the remaining goroutines. Network I/O uses the integrated netpoller, so a goroutine waiting on a socket does not occupy a thread at all.

items.title: append and shared backing arrays
items.question: a := make([]int, 3, 10); b := append(a, 1); c := append(a, 2). What is b[3]?
items.answer: 2. a has spare capacity, so both appends write into the same backing array at index 3, and the second overwrites the first. A slice is a view (pointer, length, capacity). Use a full slice expression a[:3:3] or copy to force a fresh allocation when results must be independent.

source.name: The Go Blog - Go Slices: usage and internals

items.title: Goroutine leaks
items.question: Why is a goroutine blocked forever on sending to an unbuffered channel effectively a memory leak?
items.answer: Blocked goroutines are never garbage collected: their stacks and everything they reference stay alive. If the receiver returned early, for example on a timeout, the sender waits forever. Select on ctx.Done() alongside the send, or use a buffered channel sized for all sends, so every goroutine has a way to exit.

items.title: Per-iteration loop variables
items.body: Since Go 1.22, each iteration of a for loop gets its own loop variable, so closures and goroutines capturing it see that iteration's value. Older code copied v := v inside the loop to get this behavior.

source.name: The Go Blog - Fixing For Loops in Go 1.22

items.title: Maps are not concurrency-safe
items.body: Built-in maps are unsafe for concurrent use when any goroutine writes; the runtime may detect this and crash with a fatal concurrent map write error. Guard maps with sync.Mutex or sync.RWMutex, or use sync.Map for mostly-append or disjoint-key workloads.

source.name: Go FAQ - Why are map operations not defined to be atomic?
